title: What Is an AI Agent?
summary: An AI agent is an LLM placed inside a loop: it reasons about a goal, takes actions with tools, observes the results, and repeats until the task is done. That loop — not the model alone — is what makes it an agent.

subtopics.title: The loop: reason → act → observe
subtopics.explanation: An agent repeatedly asks the model 'what should I do next?', executes the chosen action, feeds the result back, and loops. The model never touches the world directly — your code runs the tool and returns an observation. This loop is the single most important idea in the whole domain.
subtopics.example:
history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
while True:
    step = llm(history)              # reason
    if step.done:
        break
    result = run_tool(step.tool, step.args)  # act
    history.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})  # observe
# the loop is the agent

subtopics.title: Tools are just functions the model can request
subtopics.explanation: A 'tool' is an ordinary function (search, calculator, DB query) described to the model by name, purpose, and argument schema. The model can't run it; it emits a request, and your code executes it. Tools are how an agent affects the real world, which is the whole point of building one.

subtopics.title: Observations close the loop
subtopics.explanation: After a tool runs, its output goes back into the conversation as an observation so the model can decide the next step with fresh information. Without feeding results back, the model is guessing blind. Observations are what let an agent adapt mid-task rather than following a fixed script.

subtopics.title: Agent vs a single LLM call
subtopics.explanation: A single call maps one prompt to one answer. An agent can take many steps, use tools, and react to what it finds — trading latency and cost for the ability to do multi-step, real-world work. If a task is one-shot (summarise this text), you don't need an agent; if it needs lookups or actions, you do.
subtopics.example:
# single call: no tools, one shot
answer = llm([{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this."}])

# agent: loops + tools until the goal is met
answer = run_agent(goal="Book the cheapest flight next Friday")

subtopics.title: Autonomy needs a stopping condition
subtopics.explanation: Because an agent decides its own next step, it can loop forever or rack up cost. Real agents cap iterations, set a token/time budget, and define a clear 'done' signal. Knowing when to stop is a safety and cost requirement, not an afterthought — it's part of what makes an agent production-ready.
subtopics.example:
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):        # hard cap
    out = llm(history)
    if out.final_answer:             # explicit done signal
        return out.final_answer
    ...
raise RuntimeError("agent did not converge")

foundations.overview: An AI agent is a large language model wrapped in a control loop that lets it pursue a goal over multiple steps: it reasons about what to do, calls tools to act, observes the results, and continues until it can answer or the task is complete. The intelligence comes from the model; the *agency* comes from the loop and the tools you give it. Understanding this loop makes every later topic — tool use, RAG, memory, orchestration — click into place.
foundations.formalDefinition: An agent is a system that uses an LLM to choose a sequence of actions (tool calls) in an environment, incorporating each action's observation into its next decision, until a termination condition is met.
foundations.whyItMatters: Most valuable real-world tasks aren't single questions — they require looking things up, calling APIs, and reacting to results. The agent loop is what turns a text predictor into something that can actually get work done, which is why 'agentic' systems are the fastest-growing use of LLMs.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the LLM as a very capable intern who can only talk: it can decide what to do and read results, but you have to physically run every tool and hand back the output. The loop is you and the intern passing notes until the job is done.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding assistants that read files and run tests, research agents that search and synthesize, customer-support agents that look up orders and issue refunds, and data agents that query warehouses — all are the same loop with different tools.
commonUseCases: Multi-step tasks needing lookups or API calls

commonMisconceptions.myth: The model runs the tools itself.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model only emits a request naming a tool and arguments. Your code executes it and returns the result — the model never has direct access to your systems.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More agent steps always means smarter results.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Extra loops add latency, cost, and chances to go off the rails. A tight loop with good tools usually beats a sprawling one; you cap steps on purpose.
A one-shot prompt→answer call is not an agent. It's only an agent when the model chooses actions and reacts to their observations over multiple steps.

interactiveWidget.title: Watch an agent think, act, and observe
interactiveWidget.caption: Step through (or auto-play) a real agent solving a two-tool task. Notice how each observation changes what it decides to do next.

config.goal: What's the weather in Paris, and should I pack an umbrella for tomorrow?

steps.thought: I need today's Paris weather first.
steps.observation: Paris: 18°C, light rain, 80% chance of showers

steps.thought: Showers are likely — but let me check tomorrow's forecast before answering.
steps.observation: Tomorrow: 16°C, rain most of the day

steps.thought: Both today and tomorrow are wet. I can answer now.

config.final: Yes — pack an umbrella. Paris is rainy today (18°C, showers likely) and tomorrow looks wet all day (16°C, rain).

checkpoints.prompt: What actually executes a tool when an agent 'calls' it?
options: Your application code runs it and returns the result
The tool runs itself on the model's servers
The user runs it manually each time
checkpoints.explanation: The model only emits a structured request (tool name + arguments). Your code runs the function and feeds the result back as an observation — the model has no direct access to your systems.

checkpoints.prompt: Which task most needs an agent (vs a single LLM call)?
options: Rewrite this paragraph in a friendlier tone
Find the cheapest in-stock laptop under $1000 and add it to my cart
checkpoints.explanation: That task needs lookups (search inventory, check stock/price) and an action (add to cart), reacting to results along the way — the multi-step, tool-using loop that defines an agent. The others are one-shot.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do production agents cap the number of loop iterations?
options: Because the model forgets after 3 steps
To bound cost/latency and prevent infinite loops
It's required by the OpenAI API
checkpoints.explanation: A self-directing loop can run forever or rack up cost if it never emits 'done'. A hard step cap (plus token/time budgets) is a basic safety and cost control.

keyTakeaways: An agent = an LLM in a loop: reason → act (tool) → observe → repeat until done.
The model decides actions but never runs them; your code executes tools and returns observations.
Feeding observations back is what lets an agent adapt mid-task instead of following a fixed script.
Use an agent only when a task needs multiple steps, lookups, or actions — not for one-shot prompts.
Always define a stopping condition (step cap + budget + explicit 'done') for safety and cost.
